slides.label: The Extrinsic Curvature of a Surface
slides.notes: Open with the chapter question from printed pages 130 through 137: how can changing normals measure curvature. The surface itself is not being measured by a ruler laid in the tangent plane; instead the Gauss map sends each point to its unit normal on the sphere, and curvature is read as signed area distortion under that map.

slides.label: The Gauss Map
slides.notes: Define the Gauss, or spherical, map as the rule assigning to each surface point its unit normal vector. Emphasize that the target is the unit sphere, not another copy of the surface. This is why extrinsic curvature sees how the surface sits in space: the measurement changes when the normal field changes.

slides.label: Curvature As Signed Area Distortion
slides.notes: Move from a single normal vector to a tiny surface patch. The Gauss map sends the patch to a patch on the sphere. Gaussian curvature is the limiting signed ratio of spherical image area to surface area. The sign is not cosmetic; it records whether the normal map preserves or reverses local orientation.

slides.label: Patch To Sphere
slides.notes: Use the saved spherical-map figure to make the ratio visible. A nearly flat surface patch has a small normal image, while a tightly bending patch sweeps a larger patch on the unit sphere. Ask students to inspect what lives in the original surface and what lives on the sphere.

slides.label: Principal Curvatures
slides.notes: At a point, every tangent direction has a normal curvature. The two extremal values are the principal curvatures kappa one and kappa two, with orthogonal principal directions. Gaussian curvature is their product, so the chapter turns the Gauss-map area ratio into the compact formula K equals kappa one times kappa two.

slides.label: Reading The Sign Of K
slides.notes: The sign catalog separates elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic, and planar behavior. Positive K means both principal bends have the same sign; negative K means opposite signs; zero K means at least one principal bend vanishes. This is a local classification, not a statement about the whole surface.

slides.label: Product Versus Average
slides.notes: Contrast Gaussian curvature with mean curvature. K equals the product of the principal curvatures and measures area distortion of the Gauss map; H equals their average and measures a different bending tendency. A saddle can have zero mean curvature while still having negative Gaussian curvature.

slides.label: Diagnostics And Common Failures
slides.notes: Turn the notebook checks into teaching discipline. A diagram must say what to inspect, and a formula must say what would fail under a bad interpretation. The saved checks confirm nonblank concept-named visuals, orientation-sensitive wedge behavior, and invariant totals such as Euler-characteristic-linked curvature accounting.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by linking the whole sequence: normals define the Gauss map, the Gauss map converts local bending into signed spherical area distortion, principal curvatures compress the measurement into K equals kappa one kappa two, and the sign of K predicts the local shape type. Preview that later chapters will compare this extrinsic-looking construction with intrinsic curvature.
